task_row_model.query: How can I implement a practical, production-ready lock-free Michael‑Scott (MS) singly linked queue in C++11 that avoids ABA and safely reclaims nodes? Explain the core enqueue/dequeue algorithm with the required atomic operations and memory_order choices, compare hazard pointers versus epoch-based reclamation for node freeing, and list common pitfalls (false sharing, memory fences, pointer tagging) and recommendations for production use.

documents.content: A simple alternative to lock-free queues is the mutex + condition-variable implementation. Threads acquire a std::mutex to mutate a linked list or circular buffer and signal consumers with std::condition_variable. This approach guarantees safety without atomic pointer semantics and makes memory reclamation trivial because the lock serializes access; nodes can be freed immediately after removal. However, it introduces blocking, priority inversion risks, and higher latency under contention. For many workloads the mutex-based queue is easier to reason about and debug than a lock-free design, and it integrates cleanly with std::unique_lock and RAII patterns.

Implementing the Michael‑Scott queue requires two atomics: head and tail pointers to nodes. Enqueue allocates a node with next=nullptr, then repeatedly reads tail and tail->next; if tail->next is null, CAS it to the new node; then CAS tail to the new node. Dequeue reads head and head->next; if head->next is null the queue is empty; otherwise read the value from head->next and CAS head to head->next. Use compare_exchange loops and atomic ops with acquire on loads of next and release on successful stores/CAS (or memory_order_acq_rel on CAS). To avoid ABA either use pointer tagging (counter with the pointer) or safe reclamation. Align head and tail to cache lines to avoid false sharing. In C++11 use std::atomic for pointers and careful compare_exchange_weak loops; never free an old head until you ensure no thread can reference it (use hazard pointers or epochs).

Hazard pointers are a safe reclamation scheme for lock‑free data structures where each thread publishes pointers it might dereference. Before accessing a node returned by an atomic load, a thread stores that pointer in its hazard slot; reclamation scans retired nodes and frees only those not present in any hazard list. Hazards allow timely reclamation without global quiescence and avoid ABA by preventing reclamation while another thread may access the node. The tradeoffs: per-thread overhead in managing hazard slots, occasional global scans when retire lists grow, and complexity to implement correct publish/unpublish semantics. Hazard pointers are well suited when threads are long‑lived and you need bounded memory for retired lists.

Reference counting via shared_ptr makes memory management simple: each node holds a std::shared_ptr to the next node so that nodes remain alive while someone can access them. This approach serializes object lifetimes with atomic reference increments and decrements, avoiding explicit reclamation schemes. However, cyclic references must be avoided, and shared_ptr atomic operations add overhead per access. In highly concurrent lock‑free queues, reference counting can introduce contention and does not address ABA on raw pointers; it may, however, be combined with weak_ptr for specific ownership patterns where cycles are impossible and atomic updates are acceptable.

Epoch‑based reclamation (EBR) uses global epochs and per‑thread announced epochs: threads entering the data structure announce an epoch; retired nodes are associated with the current epoch and only reclaimed once all threads have advanced beyond that epoch. EBR has low per‑operation overhead and batches frees, but it depends on threads making forward progress: a stalled thread prevents reclamation and causes memory retention. Implementations add periodic epoch advances and scanning of per‑thread epoch announcements. Compared with hazard pointers, EBR is cheaper in steady state but less robust when threads can be paused unpredictably (e.g., due to preemption or blocking system calls).
